report:
Based on this research, here's my assessment:

## Conclusion
There is **moderate, but nuanced** evidence for this claim. Anti-cytokine drugs do appear to reduce depressive symptoms in people with chronic inflammatory conditions (like rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease), but the effect is likely driven largely by improvement in the underlying physical illness rather than a direct antidepressant action, and benefits are concentrated in people with elevated baseline inflammation.

## Key Evidence

**Supporting the claim:** The most authoritative source is Kappelmann et al.'s systematic review and meta-analysis (Molecular Psychiatry, 2016), which pooled RCTs of anti-cytokine drugs (mainly anti-TNF agents) used in inflammatory conditions where depressive symptoms were a secondary outcome. It found a significant overall antidepressant effect compared to placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/, https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167). Notably, however, meta-regression found no significant association between improvement in depressive symptoms and improvement in the physical illness itself, suggesting a possibly independent (not merely secondary) effect.

**Complicating/contradicting evidence:** When anti-cytokine drugs (infliximab) were tested directly for *treatment-resistant depression* (not comorbid with inflammatory disease), the pivotal RCT by Raison et al. found **no overall benefit** over placebo — improvement was seen only in the subgroup with high baseline CRP (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10942546/, psychiatryonline.org summary). A follow-up meta-analysis of infliximab in treatment-resistant depression similarly concluded it was not broadly efficacious, again only helping those with elevated inflammatory markers (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091305719303521). This indicates effects are inflammation-dependent, not universal.

## Bottom Line
The claim is reasonably well-supported for populations with chronic inflammatory disease and elevated inflammatory markers, but should be qualified: effects are modest, heterogeneous across drug classes/conditions, and strongest in high-inflammation subgroups rather than universal across all patients.
